#3288. John Ternus talks plans to improve Siri AI

During Apple’s quarterly earnings call, CEO John Ternus was asked repeatedly about Siri AI’s future. Here’s what he said about Apple’s plans for improving and expanding Siri AI.

Sometimes when Apple launches a new feature or product, the company sees its work as finished, and whatever ships goes unchanged for far too long. Many might characterize Siri this way, arguing the assistant went years without meaningful improvement or updates.

But according to Apple CEO John Ternus, the Siri AI that just shipped is only the beginning of what’s planned.

Yesterday on Apple’s quarterly earnings call, Ternus gave a rundown of Siri AI’s capabilities. He concluded: “We’re really excited to have rolled all these innovations out, and there’s still so much more we plan to do.”

This signals that Apple doesn’t see Siri AI as a feature that can now be left alone for a while. Instead, as we already saw in iOS 27.2 last week, Apple is focused on rapidly improving it.

Now that Siri AI is out, I would like to see it iterate as follows:

Support for a wider range of file types, such as PDF.

Accessing it from Search (especially on the Mac) should be instantaneous and reliable.

Proactively suggesting and reminding the user based on what it knows.

What are those future plans? It sounds like agentic capabilities may be among them. Ternus said:

With Siri AI, we really have the kind of—the Siri we always wanted. It’s primarily request-based today, but as we talked about at WWDC, it’s built on a modern, orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand capabilities over time.

It’s telling that Ternus says Siri is “primarily request-based today” and mentions “room to expand capabilities” before pivoting to mention agentic features. It sounds like Apple is already, behind-the-scenes, envisioning and working toward a version of Siri that won’t need to be “primarily request-based.”

Finally, later in the call when discussing opportunities for services growth, including potentially launching new services, Ternus says: “We think intelligence is going to be another opportunity as well.” This refers back to an earlier discussion of Apple’s intent to charge a fee for expanded usage limits on certain Siri AI and Apple Intelligence capabilities. The idea is that as Siri evolves and improves, Apple will have opportunities to charge for certain features.

What are your takeaways from Ternus’s comments on Siri AI? Let us know in the comments.

#3286. Apple Wallet driver’s licenses coming to three new states soon

Apple Wallet driver’s licenses recently launched in Virginia and Oklahoma, but three more states are expected to follow soon, bringing us close to 20 US states on board.

Digital IDs are becoming far more common than they were when Apple first added support in the Wallet app back in 2021. And today, 16 US states plus Puerto Rico support the feature on iPhone.

The latest additions, Virginia and Oklahoma, debuted just in the last couple months.

And it looks like three more states will be coming soon:

This summer evidence was discovered of both Utah and Virginia being added to Apple’s backend for driver’s license support. Virginia has since gone live, so it’s expected that Utah will launch as one of the next supported states.

Kentucky previously announced it will support Apple Wallet driver’s licenses after upgrading its digital ID system this summer. All indications are that the upgrade has been completed, so based on the state’s original plans, we should see licenses in Apple Wallet soon.

North Carolina recently announced the launch of its new digital driver’s license system. As part of the announcement, it confirmed licenses will be supported in Apple Wallet by early 2027.

Additional states might always surprise us and launch in Wallet before Utah, Kentucky, or North Carolina. We’ve seen a clear acceleration of states signing on to offer Wallet driver’s licenses.

But for now at least, the three states above appear the strongest candidates to debut soon.

#3284. iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving

iOS 27.2 arrived last week with a variety of new features and changes for iPhone. Here are two new iOS 27.2 features I’ve been loving lately.

I’ve used Apple Podcasts for the last few years after previously sticking with third-party apps. The native Podcasts app won me over with excellent features like transcripts and automatic chapters.

My main hesitation in recommending the Podcasts app, however, has been its confusing Up Next queue. Thankfully, iOS 27.2 delivers a long-awaited fix.

In iOS 27.2, the Home tab in Apple Podcasts splits Up Next into two separate sections: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

These new sections offer, in my view, a much better system than what was there before. I no longer lose track of episodes I’ve previously started, since they’re not getting replaced by new episodes in my queue. Instead, there’s a clear divide between what’s new and what’s in-progress.

Shared Albums have long been one of my favorite features in Apple Photos. I don’t post on social media often, but I do love sharing photos and videos with close family and friends via the Photos app.

iOS 27 brought big upgrades to Shared Albums, the first notable changes in years. And to my surprise, Apple has already introduced even more improvements with iOS 27.2. Per Apple:

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos

Support for editing captions and comments is long overdue, but a welcome addition. I also love the prompt that helps prevent duplicate photos, because I always find myself needing to double-check if I’ve shared certain photos already—now I don’t have to anymore.

The hope for a hole-free design is now hanging by a thread

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's already been lots of rumors about how Apple will redesign the iPhone 20 and commemorate the 20th anniversary of the original iPhone's release. One of the most prominent rumors claims that the device could feature an all-glass design, with no cutouts or notches for the camera and Face ID hardware.

However, according to leaker Digital Chat Station, the iPhone 20's display will indeed feature holes for the Dynamic Island. He doesn't go into much detail about this particular design feature, but it's not all that surprising now that we've seen the iPhone Duo.

The rumors had claimed the iPhone 20 would hide the camera and Face ID beneath the screen, enabling the first truly full-screen iPhone experience. This was expected to tie into the curved glass design, which was rumored to include curved edges to simulate the appearance of a glass phone.

Of course, a Dynamic Island cutout means that illusion isn't going to be quite so convincing. You can't claim "all-glass" when there's an obvious hole at the top of the screen.

Of course, the problem with under-display camera technology is that the screen is in the way. Apple has made some headway: The iPhone Duo has an under-display FaceTime camera, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max moved Face ID's IR camera beneath the screen.

But the Duo's FaceTime camera is not great — with a resolution of 4 megapixels — and it certainly isn't the kind of camera you'd want to take selfies with. That's a common problem with under-display cameras, and it seems even Apple hasn't been able to figure out how to compensate for it.

Obviously, the Duo already has a 12MP front camera, as well as the ability to shoot selfies by combining the rear cameras with the outer display — so it's not a huge loss. But since the iPhone 20 won't be able to do any of those things, it seems unlikely that an under-display camera will be up to scratch.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

This is a disappointing leak, and while there's no telling how things may actually pan out over the next several months, it makes sense that the iPhone 20 will keep the Dynamic Island around. The only question I have is whether the Dynamic Island will stay the same size, or if Apple will manage to trim it down even more.

Are you excited for a near all-glass iPhone 20? Sound off in the comments.

The Motley Fool is the O.G. stock and investment advice website, dating back to the early days of the Internet, when WIRED’s website was still called hotwired.com. It started as a tip sheet in the early ‘90s by brothers Tom and David Gardner, and it rode a wave of hype to become a cult phenomenon, viewed with equal interest and skepticism by the established investment class. Thirty years and a whole bunch of books later, The Motley Fool now feels like the established investment class, with a Stock Advisor subscription service offering stock tips that were shown in a 2017 study led by Penn State to consistently beat the S&P 500.

The Motley Fool is not a single service. Rather, it’s a suite of stock-tips and analysis services, packaged in different bundles. The three main tiers are Stock Advisor ($199), Epic ($499), and Epic Plus ($1,999). Each higher tier offers more stock tips per month, more comprehensive data and research on potential investments, and more sophisticated analysis tools. The Epic Plus tier also offers access to “moneymaker” investment portfolios that are touted to follow Warren Buffett’s investment strategy. Generally, the site advises beginning investors with smaller portfolios to stick to the basic Stock Advisor tips to start out. The Fool also tends to recommend buying at least 50 stocks and holding them for at least 5 years, so it’s not a day-trading tool. Today, Motorola has shared a whole lot more info on its brand-new Signature 27 — packing the new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 I tested and a retina-searing 12,000-nit display. But not only will it test your eyes, it will test the limits of your wallet.

This is a $1,599 phone. Yowzers. Pre-sales will go live on November 16.

Motorola, the company that has spent the last decade charming us with accessible mid-range and affordable phones, has jumped straight into the ultra-flagship pool. And to justify this phone compared to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, it built a device with a spec sheet that's absurdly overpowered.

If you’re going to charge $1,600 for a slab phone in this economy, you have to throw the kitchen sink at it. Turns out Motorola chucked the entire plumbing system in there for good measure — packing it all into a rather suave, slimline design.

Let’s start with the screen — a 1.5K Extreme AMOLED Duo tandem display that peaks at a bonkers 12,000 nits of brightness. For context, Motorola says users can “comfortably view” this “on a sunny afternoon,” but it’s closer to being able to read a map on the surface of the sun.

And for when you do want to flashbang your eyeballs with TikTok, there’s Bang & Olufsen-tuned speakers, too!

Under the hood is that Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, which as you know from my testing is an absolute monster. This is kept from melting your hands by an ArcticMesh cooling system with a massive vapor chamber.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

And to keep that silicon running, Motorola’s crammed in a gargantuan 7,000 mAh silicon-carbon battery that supports 90W wired charging and 50W wireless charging.

To further justify that astronomical price tag, Motorola strapped a camera block to the back of the phone that is bordering on clinical insanity. I’ll be real with you, it does look a bit weird to me. But I promise it’s functions are crazy.

The main shooter is a 50MP Sony sensor with a massive f/1.6 aperture designed to suck in as much light as physically possible. Next to it is a 50MP ultrawide, but the real flex is the 200MP periscope sensor capable of 100x Super Zoom Pro.

Need to take a selfie? That’s also a 50MP sensor, capable of shooting full 4K video.

But the wildest addition in my eyes is the industry’s first dedicated EVS “Action Sensor.” It’s not a camera; it’s a dedicated piece of hardware whose sole job is to detect pixel-level light intensity changes to freeze fast-moving subjects without blurring. Think of it like the equivalent of having a super fast shutter speed — something that’s a rarity in smartphones.

Pair that with Dolby Vision support and an AI video enhancement engine that optimizes dynamic range in real-time, and you effectively have a full camera rig in your pocket.

The Signature 27 is explicitly designed to run Gemini Intelligence and the brand’s own Qira AI ecosystem. To run the multi-step AI agents locally, Motorola needed to boost the RAM, which they’ve done in a rather clever way.

In silicon, you’ve got up to 16GB LPDDR5X, but with the RAM boost feature, that can be scaled up to a staggering 24GB of memory — utilizing some of the on-board storage.

This paves the way to a clever hybrid system where Gemini handles the super complex generative stuff, but local model work is entirely possible too. However, it does explain why the retail price has been driven into the stratosphere.

The Motorola Signature 27 is looking set to be a gorgeous, hyper-capable device that will likely outspec almost everything else released.

But it is also a 12,000-nit warning sign. Between Apple’s price hikes and Motorola’s $1,599 super slab, the era of an “affordable flagship killer” is behind us. If you want top-tier specs in this market, there’s quite the premium to pay.

#3274. Chernobyl’s Dogs May Be Evolving, but Scientists Don’t Know Why

The dogs living near the disaster site of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant are not like other dogs—at least as far as their genomes go. In recent years, researchers uncovered a unique genetic profile among this population, but what’s driven this distinction remained unclear.

The explanation that’s perhaps most tantalizing to a sci-fi author is that the persistent radiation at the nuclear site has caused mutations to accumulate in the dogs’ genomes. But there are other ways a population’s genetics can change over time, such as random drift or natural selection. A recent study published in the scientific journal Genes revisited these pups, searching for genetic patterns pointing to one of these processes.

The researchers compared the DNA from dogs living in the area right around the nuclear plant with genetic material from dogs living in the city of Chernobyl, about 16 kilometers away. They also compared these canines to other global dog populations. The contrast alone was extreme. The dogs in Chernobyl city “are more genetically similar to dogs in the Galapagos Islands than they are to the dog population” at the nuclear plant, said Megan Dillon, a postdoctoral researcher at North Carolina State University and first author of the study.

But more striking still, the comparison revealed that random chance alone could not explain the differences between the dog populations. Instead, it seems the dogs at the nuclear site have been experiencing natural selection.

“When I was first doing those analyzes, I had to kind of pause and was like, ‘Wow, I have to make sure I'm doing all of this right,’ because this is very interesting, very surprising,” Dillon said.

Not only did the dogs seem to be evolving, but some of the genomic regions under the highest selective pressure were associated with functions such as DNA repair, immunity, and cell survival. In other words, certain genetic differences in the dogs from the plant could be relevant for coping with environmental stress.

Instead of being mutations, these genomic variants likely already existed among local dogs but became more common in the population over the past 40 years. “These dog populations already had this high degree of genetic diversity,” Dillon said. “Maybe this founding population at the power plant had the kind of genetic toolkit to endure and survive in these harsh conditions. It’s not necessarily that they were being bombarded with new mutations.”

Taken together, the results support the hypothesis that natural selection contributed to the difference seen in the dogs at Chernobyl compared to other populations. What remains unclear is which environmental factors favored these variants and whether they provide any specific advantage. “Even though we found this evidence of selection and it is around these biologically relevant genes, we still cannot say that this is tied to the exposures that the dogs have faced,” Dillon noted.

Radiation at the disaster site might seem like the easiest explanation to point to, but there are many other selective pressures this dog population has faced since nuclear meltdown. Chernobyl’s dogs are descended from pets left behind during the evacuations. Since then, they’ve persisted through Ukraine’s harsh winters and weathered other pollutants including heavy metals and pesticides also deposited in the area. “A lot of these contaminants have similar signatures and similar pathology,” Dillon said. “There are just too many different things to really be able to tease apart a single variable.”

The researchers also don’t have access to longitudinal samples that would show exactly how this population has changed over time. “It's almost like looking at a single still image and trying to figure out what came before it,” said Matthew Breen, a professor of genomics at North Carolina State University and the study’s senior author. “Those first few years were probably the most critical period—if they were selected, that's when that selection process would have happened.”

It’s not possible to go back and get samples from the dogs who lived there in 1986, a time when no organism—not even a bacterium—had its full genome sequenced. Breen was a graduate student in England then. “I was involved in a project driving around the Welsh mountain hills, collecting sheep from the pastures because the radioactive cloud had blown over Western Europe,” he recalled. There wasn’t anything to see in the data gathered then, but the technology has evolved, and those sheep had also not been living at the center of a nuclear meltdown for generations.

Nearly four decades after the accident, the Chernobyl exclusion zone has also become a refuge for wildlife. Wolves, deer, wild boars, and lynx now roam the area—a return that researchers largely attribute to the decline in human activity. Among some of these residents, such as the wolf population, researchers have also observed similar genomic distinctions to those seen in the dogs.

“It really demonstrates the resilience of nature to catastrophic events caused by humans,” Breen said. “You push something in one direction, it can respond to that and either push back or deviate its path going forward. I think this is what we're seeing here.”

#3272. Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.

Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.

The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.

When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.

You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.

Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.

Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.

If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.

Gym Strength requires an iPhone running iOS 27.3 or an iPad running iPadOS 27.3. An Apple Watch running watchOS 27.3 optionally lets you view exercises and log reps and weight from your wrist, while tracking heart rate and calories burned.

Gym Strength also introduces Training Note, an optional feature powered by Apple Intelligence that previews workouts, explains progression, and highlights milestones. Training Note requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad with the device set to English.

Gym Strength is included in the existing Fitness+ subscription. It joins a library of trainer-led workouts spanning 12 workout types, including Strength, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Core, Cycling, Rowing, Dance, Kickboxing, treadmill walking and running, and Mindful Cooldown.

Fitness+ also offers guided meditations, personalized recommendations, and Custom Plans for scheduling workouts, with new sessions added every week.

Fitness+ is also included in Apple One Premier, which costs $39.95 per month in the U.S. and bundles Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud+ storage.

#3271. The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed

Author and Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst next to his new Digit 5 humanoid robot worker.

Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.

Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.

We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.

With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?

Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.

Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.

ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics

Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.

Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.

As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.

After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.

I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.

I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.

Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility

We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.

While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok

I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.

Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.

Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok

Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.

Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.

Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.

The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics

Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.

All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.

The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.

When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics

Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.

With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.

I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok

But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.

We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.

I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.

With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

This article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

Jonathan W. Hurst is the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics and a robotics professor at Oregon State University.

This is the most honest account I've read from a robotics founder. While Tesla and Figure are still showing demos, Agility has actually deployed robots in real customer environments, moved over 100,000 totes at GXO, and hit 98% accuracy at Schaeffler. Digit 5's specs are driven entirely by what customers need: 20 hours of work per day, 9-minute charge, 23 kg lift to 1.75 m shelves. That's real engineering for real problems. The tension between engineering vision and commercial reality is something every robotics founder will face. Professor Hurst lays it out without spin.

Why humanoid though? In particular, why bi-pedal? Why use legs at all? Are wheels surely better and easier? Legs seem like unnecessary complexity. Wheels on 'legs" for suspension can be a great alternative. I don't understand the obsession with humanoid form?

It seems to me that even at scale production, the robot we employ in industry should do jobs people cannot. Highly radioactive, highly toxic, and factors where the atmosphere needs to be unsuitable for humans. i.e., oxygen-deprived environment or low pressure/vacuum. Or use them on the 3rd shift when people are less willing to work.

Robots should increase manufacturing that was impossible to do in the past. We should be exploring new types of manufacturing, not replacing people in manufacturing that humans can do. That's how you create growth.

#3270. Numica raises $21M to buy accounting firms from retiring US owners

Roosh X and Flashpoint backed the New York start-up, which has bought seven practices since launching in June 2025.

Numica co-founders Victor Lysenko (left) and Slava Orekoff

Numica, a New York start-up that buys small accounting firms from owners close to retirement, has raised $21M to buy more of them.

The capital, a mix of equity and debt, comes from Roosh X and Flashpoint Capital, the company said.

Once a deal closes, Numica moves the firm’s clients, staff and daily work onto its own AI system. The platform keeps the books and handles billing, practice management and tax filing, while accountants check the AI’s output instead of doing the work by hand.

For clients, however, little should change. They keep the same accountant and the same relationship, because the changes happen behind the scenes.

Numica focuses on firms with annual revenue of $700,000 to $5m. Practices of that size are easier to take over, and they are usually too small to interest larger buyers.

Most of their clients are local businesses such as restaurants, hair salons, and dental practices.

The company launched in June 2025 and bought its first practice in New York a few months later.

According to Numica, that firm’s profit margin rose from 37% to 52% within two months, and it expects the figure to reach 70%. It has since bought seven practices in total.

“The model is simple: we acquire a profitable business and make it more profitable,” said Slava Orekoff, Numica’s co-founder and chief executive.

Behind the bet is a shortage of accountants. More than 300,000 US accountants and auditors left their jobs over two years, a fall of 17%, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2023. As a result, many small-firm owners have no one inside the business to take over and no obvious buyer.

At the same time, private equity has moved into the sector, though mostly at the top. Ten of the 20 largest US accounting firms are or will soon be backed by private equity.

Numica, by contrast, is aiming at the much smaller firms that those investors tend to pass over.

Flashpoint, a London-based investor, first backed Numica with equity and has now added a growth debt loan. Ilja Velickis, associate partner at Flashpoint Growth Debt, said the facility gives the company more money to speed up its acquisitions.

Orekoff, a former senior vice president at SAP, founded Numica with Victor Lysenko, who previously founded and ran Osome, a Singapore-based accounting start-up.

#3269. What’s the Difference Between an Ebike and an E-Moto?

The good: US sales are way up from the start of the decade, after the pandemic sparked interest in two-wheelers and helped riders go farther, faster, and with less effort. More people also see ebikes as viable transportation options and as more affordable and accessible alternatives to increasingly expensive cars. The bad? Sales are down from two years ago, and bike manufacturers and sellers have suffered. Riding injuries are up, notably among children, and lawmakers are looking for ways to control them.

Part of the issue is that people struggle to understand the difference between types of ebikes, and between ebikes and their faster cousins, e-motos. This often isn’t their fault. Lawmakers and vehicle retailers themselves have blurred the edges of the product categories, even though many places require riders of the most powerful ebikes and e-motos to meet age, licensing, and registration requirements.

Today, a kid might see a targeted ad online for an electric dirt bike capable of speeds exceeding 40 mph and ask their parents to buy it straight from the internet—neither understanding that no one, much less a minor, is legally allowed to pilot them on public streets without a license.

Here’s a handy guide to the different types of electric micromobility vehicles available, to help you keep them straight. Local laws vary, so buyers should research and understand what’s allowed on their local roads before whipping out a credit card.

The electric bicycle industry uses three “classes” to differentiate product capabilities. Class 1 ebikes have motors that kick in when the rider pedals—the assist stops at 20 mph. Class 2 ebikes also have this “pedal assist” functionality, plus throttles, so riders can travel up to 20 mph without pedaling at all. Class 3 ebikes have more powerful pedal assist that stops helping at 28 mph. (In some places, this limit is 25 mph.)

Thirty-nine US states incorporate these three-class systems in their laws. In general, they require Class 3 riders to wear helmets and be at least 16 years old. Some states require riders to be at least 14 or 15 to ride any ebike at all. Outside of the laws, ebikes are mostly regulated like standard bicycles, and riders must follow the same rules of the road.

Most states don’t require a license or registration to ride ebikes. As of 2026, New Jersey and Alaska are the two exceptions. New Jersey requires registration and licensing for all ebikes, and insurance for Class 3 ebikes. Alaska, meanwhile, has no statewide ebike laws, and some locales, including Anchorage, require licenses for ebikes with sustained output over 750 watts, which can generally hit between 20 and 28 mph.

When shopping for an ebike, buyers should keep an eye on motor wattage levels. Entry-level ebikes typically have 250-watt motors and are great for commuting and flatter leisure riding. Upgrade to 500 watts to reach about 20 mph with a throttle and ride up moderate hills; 750 watts is generally the legal limit for street-appropriate ebikes and is great for bigger hills and heavier loads. Vehicles that are 1,000 watts and over aren’t considered ebikes and are usually sold for off-roading and riding on private property.

Those 1,000-watt devices? Despite some manufacturers’ marketing claims, they aren’t legally bikes but e-motos or mopeds. E-motos don’t need to have operable pedals—in fact, sometimes manufacturers or riders add fake ones to make them appear as ebikes. They are throttle-dependent rather than pedal-assist. They can have between 1,000 and 6,000 watts of motor power and can reach top speeds of 60 mph.

Because these vehicles are more powerful, many states require riders to register them and obtain a license and insurance—just like motorcycles. In most places, the process for getting one of these licenses looks a lot like getting a car license. Riders can get permits or junior licenses at 16 or 17 years old and often must be legal adults to get a full license.

Beyond looking at a two-wheeled vehicle’s specs, e-motos have other visual tells. Ebikes have a classic slender bicycle-like frame; observers should be able to see clear “daylight” through the body of the device. They have slimmer tires and rear fenders that hug their back tires. E-motos are chunkier, with wide midsections and substantial battery packs, which block most “daylight.” They have substantial coil shocks to absorb road impacts. They usually have wide, knobby tires and big rear fenders that sit high above their wheels. E-motos often have fixed foot pegs, like motorcycles, versus classic pedals.

There’s a final, tricky twist. Many ebikes are electronically speed-limited and can be hacked to go faster via (often easily available) software modifications. Some can be modified physically, by strategically moving sensors or cutting wires. These changes can turn a once-legal ebike street-illegal. That can not only void a device's warranty but also strain other components, risking failure.

PeopleForBikes, a US trade organization, warns that some manufacturers enable this sort of dodge by putting pedals on e-motos and calling them ebikes. These vehicles can be easily “unlocked” or come with “off-road” modes that let them travel much faster.

“E-motos are motor vehicles,” the group says.

#3264. AI super PACs lost their biggest general election bet of the midterms

AI super PACs spent $79M across 68 seats this cycle. Leading the Future, the biggest network, ends it with just over $20M left, and most Republicans backed by either camp lost.

United States Capitol, First Street Southeast, Washington, DC, USA

The AI industry’s biggest bet on a competitive general election race lost on Tuesday. Two super PACs linked to Leading the Future spent $4.8M backing Republican Darline Graham in South Carolina’s Senate race. She lost to Democrat Annie Andrews, who had called her “Data Center Darline”.

Most Republicans backed by either side of the AI industry’s spending fight lost, Fortune found in its tally of the closest races. It was the same night voters rejected AI data centres in 40 of 41 ballot measures. AI super PACs spent $79M across 68 House and Senate seats this cycle, according to Tech Influence Watch, a tracker run by writer Molly White.

The money comes from two networks. Leading the Future wants light regulation and a single national AI rulebook that overrides state laws. Andreessen Horowitz co-founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz gave it $25M each, according to filings reviewed by Fortune. OpenAI president Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, are also among its biggest donors.

Public First, which has significant backing from Anthropic, wants stronger safeguards. Both networks run one arm for each party.

Leading the Future launched in August 2025 with a war chest of around $100M, WIRED reported. It ends the cycle with just over $20M in the bank. In October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said AI money in politics was clearly not working.

The biggest fight came in June, in the Democratic primary for New York’s 12th District. Leading the Future spent more than $8.1M against Assemblymember Alex Bores, a co-author of the state’s RAISE Act. Public First spent about $15M backing him. Bores lost, finishing second to Micah Lasher, who also campaigned on AI safety.

Leading the Future then spent about $10M in the general election, mostly on safe seats, WIRED reported. Its Republican arm, American Mission, spent $590,428 backing Aaron Flint in Montana’s 1st District and $509,067 behind Laurie Buckhout in North Carolina’s 1st. Both conceded. Its Democratic arm, Think Big, backed Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz, who won.

Public First’s Republican arm had a similar night. Defending Our Values spent $1.49M backing Carlos De La Cruz in Texas’s 35th District and $974,908 behind Rhett Marques in Alabama’s 2nd. Both lost. It also spent $857,426 backing Scott Singer against Moskowitz. Its Democratic arm, Jobs and Democracy, backed two winners in Ohio and Pennsylvania.

A conservative AI group, Alliance for a Better Future, spent just over $1M backing Mike Rogers in Michigan and $810,000 behind Susan Collins in Maine, Molly White wrote. Both lost.

Guardrails Alliance, a tech worker group pushing for stricter rules, spent more than $1M each against Flint and California Rep. Jimmy Gomez, TechCrunch reported. Gomez lost to Angela Gonzales-Torres.

Groups pushing for stronger rules claimed the result.

“Voters in both parties delivered the same verdict tonight. This is a crushing blow to the AI industry’s anti-regulatory efforts to buy a Congress that would look the other way.” Brad Carson, Public First Action, to WIRED

“Allying with the worst parts of the AI industry is just kryptonite for a campaign, and the results tonight double down on that.” Alex Bores, to Politico

Charlie Blaettler, Guardrails Alliance’s political director, told TechCrunch that Leading the Future held back in close races because its money would have become a liability for its candidates.

“Our goal is to make AI money politically toxic.” Charlie Blaettler, Guardrails Alliance, to TechCrunch

Before the vote, Leading the Future told TechCrunch that primaries are a better use of its money, because spending there builds name recognition and helps candidates set AI agendas. It said it would keep spending in 2028. It also leaves the cycle with dozens of winning candidates from both parties, WIRED noted, most of them in safe seats.

A Republican lobbyist pointed to the party’s message on AI.

“It’s proven to be incredibly unpopular, and ‘beat China’ did not resonate at all in places that it really needed to.” Greta Joynes, Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, to Politico

Bores is already preparing for the next round. His new nonprofit, Who Decides, aims to raise $30M before 2028, Fortune reported.

#3263. iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 add Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more to Safari

Apple just released the first betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3, with some big changes to Safari. The updates add a new vertical tab layout, Adaptive Dark Mode, and Siri AI Custom Actions.

Safari in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 is adding a new Vertical Tabs design option. If you choose this design, you’ll see your tabs arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari rather than along the top, as in the traditional Safari design.

By default, Vertical Tabs show as icons in order to maximize vertical and horizontal space. If you’d like, you can also resize the tab bar to see website titles.

To try Vertical Tabs in the new iOS 27.3 beta, head to the Settings app, choose Apps, tap Safari, then look for the new Vertical Tabs option. On Mac and iPad, the feature can also be enabled via the “View” menu in the Safari app directly.

Vertical tab layouts have become an increasingly popular web browser feature. Arc from The Browser Company popularized the option. Arc, however, ceased development last year, and The Browser Company announced last month that it will discontinue it altogether in December.

If you regularly visit a website that doesn’t support Dark Mode, Apple’s next round of software updates adds Adaptive Dark Mode. This will automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t support the feature.

If Dark Mode is enabled on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac and you visit a website that doesn’t support it, you’ll see a new “Try” button. If you tap this, Safari will automatically create a Dark Mode version of the website.

You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

Finally, Siri AI can now take direct action on tabs in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3. This includes things like using Siri to move, sort, organize, and close your tabs.

In a future update, Siri’s on-screen awareness will also expand to include the entire content of a website, not just what’s visible on the screen at a particular moment.

iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3 are rolling out to developers for beta testing today. The update will likely be released to everyone sometime in December. What do you think of these new Safari features? Will you try out the new Vertical Tabs feature? Let us know down in the comments.

#3262. New Jersey’s New Ebike Law Is Causing Chaos

In January, outgoing New Jersey governor Phil Murphy signed a first-in-the-nation bill that sought to make roads safer for everyone.

S-4834, passed by a wide bipartisan margin and sponsored by state Senate president Nick Scutari, was motivated by the “dramatic increase” in ebike use, which “created greater dangers for their operators, other motorists, and pedestrians,” Scutari wrote in a statement. Several teenagers in his district and elsewhere in the state had died on two-wheeled motorized vehicles, including a 13-year-old boy who died last fall after colliding with a landscaping truck.

The new law requires anyone who owns and rides a bike with pedal-assist tech or a throttle to be at least 15 years old and to have a license, either a driver’s license or a motorized bicycle license. (Riders can receive a stand-alone motorized bicycle only after passing a road test.) Riders must register their ebikes with the state’s Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC), and anyone on a bike that can travel faster than 20 mph must have insurance.

Now advocates in the state and elsewhere in the country say that one of the country’s first big experiments with ebike licensing is a slow-moving mess. Riders reported widespread confusion at local MVC branches, where workers have appeared uninformed about the new rules and have even reportedly run out of registration stickers. People with years-old ebikes who can’t provide proof of purchase have been told to pay sales tax again. Agency buildings lack bike parking and are hard to reach by public transit. Enforcement of the law is spotty and inconsistent. Ebike-loving vacationers have reported avoiding the state altogether. And ebike sales, which boomed during the pandemic, have fallen off a cliff.

“They have vilified ebikes,” says Scott Chambers, owner of Zippy’s Bikes in Wildwood, New Jersey. His store has seen a 90 percent annual decline in ebike sales and a 50 percent overall decline. With most of last year’s inventory unsold, the shop’s future is “bleak,” he says. “It’s hard to play catch-up.” The New Jersey E-Bike Coalition, which formed in response to this law, says 37 bike shops have closed statewide.

New Jersey is just one of many places grappling with questions about ebikes. Across the country, reports of reckless riding, speeding, and dangerous collisions, especially among teenagers, have lawmakers looking for new ways to crack down on motor-assisted bikes. Lawmakers in California, Illinois, and New York have proposed their own ebike licensing schemes, though none have passed. New York’s City Council backed down from a licensing proposal this summer.

At the same time, workers, leisure riders, and everyday errand-runners have come to depend on ebikes, which are cheaper to buy, fuel, and store than cars. “I’m a little bit in limbo,” says Karin Vanoppen, a Jersey City resident who hasn’t ridden her pedal-assisted bike, which she uses to scale steep hills and pick up groceries, since the state began enforcing the rule in July. Vanoppen doesn’t have a driver’s license—she has never needed one—and says the state’s testing locations are all more than an hour's ride away, some on roads where ebikes aren’t legally allowed to ride. At a legislative hearing, one lawmaker suggested that those who can’t drive ask their parents to transport them to their ebike road tests. “I guess my 85-year-old mother has to come,” Vanoppen says.

New Jersey has issued 16,825 ebike registrations, New Jersey MVC spokesperson William Connolly told WIRED, a small fraction of the estimated 300,000 ebikes and e-motos that advocates say are in the state. MVC has granted 221 ebike licenses. In a written statement, Connolly acknowledged that the state agency underwent “an adjustment period as our staff is trained, and both staff and customers get used to new procedures.” Overall, though, “the launch has gone smoothly,” he said. (Several state ebike riders with driver’s licenses told WIRED they had no trouble registering their bikes.)

Persistent public confusion over what an ebike is complicates matters. The lowest-speed models use motors that propel only when riders pedal and top out at 20 mph; the fastest have throttles or more powerful motors that can reach 25 to 28 mph. E-motos, a different and newly popular vehicle category, can forgo pedals and hit much higher speeds, sometimes past 50 mph. They also exist in a legal gray area, either unregulated or subject to licensing, registration, and age requirements that are rarely enforced.

Even police officers can struggle to tell the two apart. Records collected through the state’s public request law by Shannon Connor, who owns the ebike shop Jesse’s E-Rides in southern New Jersey, show that at least five of the eight vehicles involved in serious crashes in the past year were e-motos, not ebikes—including the collision that killed a 13-year-old last fall. New Jersey has treated motorized vehicles like e-motos and mopeds as motorcycles for decades: Riders must be at least 17 and have a license. (In Southern California, which has similar laws, at least 12 parents have been charged after prosecutors accused them of knowingly allowing their children to operate electric, two-wheeled vehicles illegally, most of them e-motos.)

“The biggest problem that we have is educating people,” Connor says. Her teenage son, Jesse, is autistic and alternates between his four red e-tricycles to travel independently. (State officials finally concluded this summer that the law doesn’t affect electric tricycles.) Her shop, named after him, has seen its sales cut in half this year and is relocating to a smaller storefront with lower rent. She says many people still don’t understand the new law and believe that ebikes have been banned altogether.

The ebike law is particularly burdensome for disabled people who can’t or don’t already drive cars, Connor says. Advocates also worry about lower-income people and delivery drivers, who may not have the time or resources to travel to get licensed. State ebike registration costs $8 annually, and licenses and exams cost $11 altogether, with all fees waived for the first year.

A new proposed bill by state senator Raj Mukherji in October would exempt lower-speed ebikes that are capable of motor-only speeds of 20 mph from insurance and licensing requirements. In a statement, Mukherji described the proposal as “a sensible balance between public safety and preserving access to affordable, environmentally friendly transportation.” So-called “class 3” ebikes, which travel faster, would continue to require licenses and registration.

Cycling advocates say there are ways to make streets safer without tighter ebike legislation. The federal government could use existing rules and regulations to crack down on e-motos, which manufacturers often sell online at lower prices and market in ways that can lead shoppers to think they’re appropriate for kids or other untrained riders.

The country could also start teaching young people to ride bikes the same way they do cars. “We want youth to be educated about how to operate vehicles safely and to know the rules of the road, and they aren’t taught that in schools in any comprehensive way,” says Ken McLeod, the policy director of the 200,000-member League of American Bicyclists. “Right now, people jump to licensing as a way to do that.”

#3261. How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written

AI-generated text is harder to spot, but that hasn’t deterred them

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor. She also covers AI and biomedical engineering.

Ellia Lebleu is a cofounder of the WikiProject AI Cleanup effort to keep Wikipedia human-written.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia.

When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material?

Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this.

Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

How do editors spot AI-generated writing today?

Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI.

Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations?

Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace.

English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through?

Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt.

Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check, which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots.

And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology.

Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working?

Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice.

What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles?

Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity.

A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else.

But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option.

Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search?

Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to.

The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?”

I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe.

A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

I feel like all of us human writers are going to have to grapple with AI-mediated readers, whether we use the AI to augment our content or our readers use AI to engage with our writing. Here's to figuring out together how to ensure our words still shine through the AI layer.

AI slop is a small problem for Wikipedia. The bigger problem is very biased editing on anything with even minimal political implication. And that's a human problem, not AI.

#3260. watchOS 27.3 beta adds new Siri Recap and Live Rewind features for Apple Watch

Apple has released the first beta of watchOS 27.3 for developers, including two new Audio Intelligence features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Apple first announced these features at its special event in September, saying they would “arrive in beta later this year.”

As a refresher, Siri Recap creates high-level summaries of conversations that you can review later. When the feature is enabled, Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title and key points that you can review in the Siri app on iPhone.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

You can turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone. When you enable it, you can set a schedule based on time and/or location, or you can manually turn it on or off. You can also access it via Control Center on Apple Watch.

Live Rewind, meanwhile, helps you recall what was just said in a conversation. You can activate Live Rewind by double-pressing the Digital Crown, and then see a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of a conversation.

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Siri Recap’s summary is described as a “brief, high-level summary of conversations,” not a transcript. Apple says it will “exclude sensitive information like financial information or government-assigned identifiers.”

Live Rewind text snippets and Siri Recap summaries are end-to-end encrypted. Apple says the features “do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple.” The company uses the S11 chip’s Secure Exclave to power the features, a “dedicated hardware-isolated compartment that processes audio in complete isolation from the rest of the system, then immediately deletes it.”

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are available in beta with watchOS 27.3, which is available now for developers.
