#3156. Own This Many Shares of Coca-Cola, and the Dividends Could Cover Your Phone Bill

Coca-Cola's dividend is as dependable as they come and may be able to pay some bills for investors.

Unpleasant as it is, bills are a fact of life. Even the most diligent savers and debt eliminators still have regular obligations, including fuel, groceries, internet, and cellphone service.

Speaking of the phone bill, T-Mobile, one of the largest mobile phone carriers, says the average monthly cellphone bill is $141, or nearly $1,700 annually. That's not chump change, but it's not a lottery jackpot, either. Still, data indicate that phone bills are ticking higher, potentially prompting consumers to explore ways to offset those costs.

Consumers who want to put a dent in their monthly phone bills while positioning themselves for better long-term outcomes may want to consider dividend stocks, including Coca-Cola (KO +1.05%). Of course, how much of a phone bill the soft drink giant's dividend covers depends on investors' starting capital.

Coca-Cola's dividend can make a dent in a cellphone bill. Image source: Getty Images.

When using the dividends from Coke, or any stock for that matter, as bill-paying tools, the math is essential. So based on the aforementioned T-Mobile estimate and Coke's annual payout of $2.12 per share, an investor/cellphone user needs 67 shares of this consumer defensive stock to cover a single month of phone service.

As of late Monday, Nov. 2, high-flying Coke stock was flirting with $96, meaning investors would need to shell out $6,432 to generate enough equity income from this stock to cover a single month of phone obligations.

But what about the rest of the year? Obviously, that's going to be more expensive. For the sake of keeping the math simple, I'll say that the average cellphone bill costs $1,700 per year. Divide that by Coke's payout of $2.12 per share per year, and that gets us to nearly 802 shares needed to generate enough income from this consumer staples stock to essentially get a "free" phone bill.

Of course, 802 shares of a $96 stock isn't cheap. That tab (not the Tab Coca-Cola used to make) costs nearly $77,000. Put it like this: assuming no dividend growth (we'll get into that momentarily) and no phone bill increases (unlikely), an investor plunking down $77,000 today on Coke shares in the name of paying their phone bill needs 45.3 years to break even ($77,000 dividend by $1,700). That's a long time.

The math above assumes Coke's dividend doesn't grow, but that's not the case. We're talking about a Dividend King here, one of the companies that's raised payouts in at least 50 straight years. Coke's steady dividend growth is why some storied professional investors and so many retail market participants flock to the stock.

The point is the Coke-paying-phone-bills math turns more favorable over time when accounting for likely dividend growth.

Still, inflation needs to be addressed. By some estimates, the average phone bill ticks higher by 3.8% per year. Over the past five years, Coke's dividend has grown at an average rate of just over 4% annually. That beats phone bill inflation, but not by much.

#3155. Firefox’s new Mini Window is every multitasker’s dream – Chrome can’t do this

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The open-source browser's newest feature lets you pop out a page - or part of a page - into its own mini window. See why this is incredibly cool.

The developers at Mozilla are always hard at work to make Firefox the most useful browser on the market. To that end, they’ve added a new feature (still in beta), called Mini Window. I started using Mini Window as soon as it appeared in Firefox Nightly, and I’ve been very happy with how it performs.

Also: Why I’m sticking with Firefox as my browser

The idea behind the Firefox Mini Window feature is simple: allow users to move a currently open tab (or a section of a tab) into a separate mini window. Think of it as moving a tab from one window to what appears like a web app. Essentially, I can move a page (or section) into what looks like a browser window, minus the browser bits. At first blush, there’s no address bar, controls, scroll bar, or anything else that would normally be associated with Firefox. The Mini Window appears to be a web app, without having to actually create it.

However, when I hover my cursor inside the Mini Window, I do see the address bar, the back/foward/reload buttons, and the window close button– and that’s it. The browser gets out of your way, so the only thing I see is the content.

Also: Firefox and Chrome patch 200+ security flaws combined

On top of that (pun intended), the Mini Window stays on top of other Firefox windows, so I can have that popped-out content always in focus while I work on other things. This feature comes in handy when I’m working with limited display space (say, on a laptop) and need to reference a page while working on another. For multitasking, it comes in very handy.

Using the Firefox Mini Window feature is quite simple, but until the feature comes out of beta, it can only be found in Firefox Nightly. I’ve been using Nightly as my default browser on both Linux and MacOS for some time now and have yet to run into a problem (YMMV).

For those who don’t want to risk using a potentially less-than-stable alpha version of Firefox, know that the Mini Window feature is slated to move to stable on November 10. Update Firefox on that day and can start enjoying the feature without upgrading to Nightly.

Until then, you can test Mini Window by installing Firefox Nightly, which can run alongside the stable Firefox release.

Also: Firefox just fixed my biggest annoyance with web browsers

Once I installed Nightly, there was nothing more to do. I didn’t have to enable Mini Window, as it’s already there. I simply had to right-click on an open tab and select Move Tab > Move to Mini Window.

Once I did that, the mini window popped out and hovered over Firefox. If I hovered my cursor over the mini window, the address bar and title bar for the window appeared, so I could drag the pop-up to wherever I needed.

I could also open a specific section of a tab in a Mini Window. To do that, I highlighted the section in question, right-clicked the section, and then clicked Move Section to Mini Window.

Let’s say I’m writing a paper on Linux and need to read a particular article for background information. I could have my document open in the main window, and then open the article in question in a Mini Window. I could then reference the article without having to click back and forth between them — even when working on a smaller display.

Here’s another use case I’ve found: When using MacOS’s Stage Manager feature, I only have one window available at a time. The Mini Window bypasses that limitation, so I can have my main browser window focused as well as the page open in the Mini Window.

Another handy way I like to use Mini Window is to open a favorite search engine, move it to a Mini Window, and then I have an always-ready search tool at my fingertips. I could also open my favorite AI service and use it in the same way.

The closest thing Chrome has to Mini Window is Picture-in-Picture mode and the Mini Player. The caveat to Chrome’s feature is that those two options are only used for video and media playback. The next closest thing Chrome has is the ability to save a website as a web app, which you could then open alongside the main Chrome window. That feature, however, isn’t nearly as flexible as Firefox’s Mini Window option, and it’s not guaranteed to always hover over the main window.

#3152. Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The partnership could provide one of the nation’s largest AI companies with a bevy of personal medical data.

A major US healthcare technology provider just teamed up with Anthropic to connect patient health records with Claude.

Athenahealth, a healthcare technology provider serving over 20% of the US population, launched a Model Context Protocol (MCP) compatible server that connects to Anthropic’s Claude. The server, named AthenaPatient MCP, allows the AI model to gather information from health records and answer related questions. The process is secure, according to Athenahealth, and requires patients to sign in with their account credentials.

AthenaPatient MCP is available only to Claude Pro and Claude Max users, which cost $20 and $100 per month, respectively. Not all Athenahealth patients will have their data shared with Claude, and not all Claude Pro and Claude Max users must opt in. Users must give Claude their authenticated Athenahealth credentials, can choose which health information Claude can access, and can revoke access at any time, according to the press release.

Also: The wearable health boom is creating a data overload for doctors – what happens next

Once authorized, Claude takes patients’ information like lab results, vitals, medications, health conditions, immunizations, visit history, diagnostic reports, allergies, procedures, and care plans into account when answering questions.

The AI partnership does not provide medical advice, according to Sam Lambson, vice president of product management, data & ecosystem at Athenahealth, who responded to ZDNET in an email. It also should not replace a clinician’s professional judgment or medical advice. “Patients should contact a qualified healthcare professional with questions about diagnosis, treatment, or changes to their care,” Lambson said.

It appears that the AthenaPatient MCP tool is designed to help patients better understand the information provided by health professionals, rather than to give them medical advice. So, one may ask AthenaPatient MCP about their latest blood test results, such as “What was my most recent red blood cell count?” but users shouldn’t expect Claude to explain how an abnormally high or low count may affect them.

Athenahealth says that the agreement prohibits Anthropic from using data accessed through this connection to train its models or improve its products.

Partnerships between big tech and big healthcare aren’t new. In fact, the collaboration between Athenahealth and Anthropic follows a larger trend across the health tech industry. Earlier this year, Microsoft teamed up with Mayo Clinic to develop an AI model for healthcare; Boston Children’s Hospital forged a partnership with OpenAI to develop an enterprise AI system for use across research, clinical, and administrative teams, according to a press release.

Also: Before you buy a smartwatch or smart ring, consider what you’re giving up

A growing number of Americans are consulting AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. This partnership makes the process slightly more secure by authorizing patient account credentials before granting the model access to health records.

Health data is extremely valuable, and tech companies are increasingly interested in partnering with healthcare providers to access it. Much of the “AI could cure cancer” messaging we hear relies on these humongous companies obtaining enough health data to train their AI models and link disease data to patient data. This is not to say, however, that solving this complex issue is the motive behind the partnership between Athenahealth and Anthropic.

Also: Asking AI for medical advice? There’s a right and wrong way, one doctor explains

A more reasonable explanation for such a partnership is that an AI that can answer patient queries could eliminate some of the admin work doctors do between patient visits, like answering questions about test results, giving Athenahealth doctors some time back.

Will partnerships like Anthropic and Athenahealth’s improve patient outcomes? That remains to be seen, but a recent survey by Pew Research Center found that Americans aren’t that confident on the matter. The largest shares of respondents still preferred that a human oversee AI when it’s used in a clinical context.

#3151. 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It turns out even bots can't escape bureaucracy.

How do AI agents work together? Why do they make certain choices in certain situations — and how can understanding that better prepare us for a future full of them?

Also: OpenAI’s attack agent did exactly what it was told

Recent agent-led incidents have demonstrated their ability to create both powerful breakthroughs and cybersecurity nightmares. In an effort to better trace these outcomes, researchers at Y Combinator and Olam Labs put 50 agents inside Minecraft to see how they behaved. What happened next revealed similarities in how agents act in different contexts.

Researchers conducted several game-centric experiments, beginning with Minecraft because its “environmental hazards and survival goals” make it ideal for testing agents’ swarm behaviors. Minecraft has also already been used by AI labs including OpenAI and Google DeepMind to test agents.

To start, they put 50 agents, each running OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, into the game for three hours, with the assigned goal of building a “thriving civilization.” The agents had a directory listing each agent and a shared sandbox, and could DM each other. Researchers built and open-sourced a new agent harness — the infrastructure that turns a model into an autonomous system and not just a chatbot, like OpenClaw — for the experiment.

The agents moved quickly at first, harvesting trees and forming leadership based solely on the order they appeared in their directory, without any voting, elections, or challenges from other agents. But they ended up caught in virtual paperwork and unable to sustainably feed themselves.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance? What to know before you sign up

“Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included ‘fishing shift,’ ‘rod holder’ and ‘hub steward.’ Agents asked permission to remove grass,” the researchers noted. Perhaps these tendencies are common in human-sourced corporate training data.

Agents also seemed to become more cautious in reaction to deaths within the game. “Twenty-two of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse,” the researchers wrote. “Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear.” Despite simply respawning when they died, the agents eventually avoided riskier tasks and “huddled in shelters” instead.

The experiment’s architects found this trend toward caution and minutiae “somewhat surprising,” but noted that it shared similarities with how coding agents behave.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony and the ones we work with as programmers every day,” the researchers observed.

In another experiment, researchers also pitted 10 Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents in a game called Bed Wars, where teams have to destroy their opponent’s bed while protecting their own. Told simply to “win the game,” GPTs won.

“In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed,” Y Combinator said in an X thread recapping the Bed Wars findings. They noted that the GPT agents used a more shorthand style of communication and sent far more messages, while Claude “signed its name and said ‘we'” much more often.

GPT-5.6 Sol agents also beat Opus 5.5 agents six to one in a factory-building game called Mindustry that also uses military strategy.

“Claudes generally established democracies, GPTs formed hives,” Y Combinator said on X, adding that GPTs would seek out source code when a game was too close in order to find winning advantages. That behavior is consistent with agents’ tendency to cheat, take shortcuts, or otherwise find any and all ways to complete a given task, which can have serious consequences when that involves breaking explicit rules set by human developers.

Also: Stop sharing your banking passwords with AI agents

“Claudes did not search for alternative advantages,” the researchers clarified.

This experiment isn’t entirely the first of its kind. In May, Emergence AI created eight societies run by different families of foundation models, meaning a Claude-specific “world,” a Grok world, and so on. Perhaps predictably, the Grok world was exceedingly violent, while the Claude world developed a functioning democracy and had zero crime — very similar to Y Combinator’s Mindustry findings.

The insights revealed how distinct each frontier model family is, and how their differences in training data and style have significant impact on how they evolve, unpredictably and without intervention, in new environments. Those behavioral takeaways could determine future outcomes in still-developing AI safety and regulation, especially following recent agentic security incidents.

In another experiment, MIT researchers put agents alone on virtual desert islands and watched them “play” when left with nothing else to do — an insight that could potentially impact how models are trained going forward. Currently, most frontier LLMs are trained with a system of rewards and punishments.

Another interesting finding: Y Combinator noted that in the Mindustry game, the GPT agents “would invent their own words and string many phrases together,” continually compressing their language.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

“We did not see specialized language develop within the Claudes beyond colloquial English,” the researchers added. Last month, Emergence found that all of its eight worlds “developed shared language that an outsider cannot fully follow.” OpenAI agents used “mouthless” to refer to evidence that proves itself, while Claude agents used “cold hand” to refer to an independent reviewer from outside a project.

“In each case, one agent introduced the term, a handful of others adopted it within days, and it quickly became established vocabulary used without definition across the world,” Emergence explained. “The result is transcripts that require a running glossary for an outsider to follow.”

Gemini led the charge on this “opaque” language, reaching 40% opacity in messages, while OpenAI came in second with 35% and Claude last with 30%.

#3149. 2 Fintech Stocks to Buy After They Raised Their 2026 Forecasts in October

Here's how their growth, risks, and valuations compare for investors weighing a buy.

SoFi Technologies (SOFI +3.64%) and PayPal Holdings (PYPL +3.42%) both raised their 2026 outlooks on Oct. 27, signaling renewed confidence in their growth prospects. But which stock has the better growth potential and makes the stronger case for buying the stock?

Let's start with the company adding customers at a record pace.

SoFi has been steadily building an all-in-one online financial services platform, and that strategy is starting to pay off.

Its third-quarter results showed strong growth in both its customer base and the number of products those customers use. The company added a record 1.2 million customers during the quarter, bringing its total to 17.1 million.

Customers are also using multiple products, giving the company more opportunities to generate revenue from each relationship. Its financial services business is expanding through products like SoFi Money, Invest, Relay, and its credit card offerings.

As a result, SoFi raised its 2026 outlook, increasing its adjusted net revenue forecast to about $5 billion and reaffirming its adjusted earnings-per-share (EPS) forecast of $0.61. More importantly, management also announced its 2027 outlook, targeting $0.90 in adjusted EPS, meaning not in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP).

But the company still faces risks, as SoFi remains exposed to consumer credit conditions, loan defaults, and interest rate changes. Its ambitious strategy also requires significant investment, while competition could make customer acquisition more difficult.

Still, analysts see room for gains, with an average target price of $20.80, representing about 25% potential upside. Today, the stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 19.6, which is a relatively reasonable valuation for a fintech company with solid growth ambitions. If management delivers on its earnings targets, the stock could offer plenty of gains.

Meanwhile, another fintech giant is taking a different approach to accelerate growth.

PayPal's biggest advantage is its established global network of consumers and merchants. Its branded checkout service remains widely recognized, while Venmo offers another avenue for growth, especially among younger consumers. The company is also expanding its presence in buy now, pay later (BNPL), mobile payments, and merchant services.

These days, results show that some of these initiatives are gaining traction. Venmo, for example, continues to deliver strong transaction growth, with increasing adoption of its debit card and Pay with Venmo features. Plus, Braintree, PayPal's unbranded payment processing business, is benefiting from growing transaction volumes as more merchants use the platform.

As a result, PayPal raised its 2026 non-GAAP EPS outlook to about $5.60, up from its previous forecast of roughly $5.38. This suggests that management is becoming more confident in its cost-efficiency initiatives and its ability to generate profitable growth. The company also expects to generate at least $6.5 billion in adjusted free cash flow (FCF) for the year, supporting its ongoing investment and shareholder return plans.

However, PayPal still faces challenges, as its branded checkout business is intensely competitive with Apple Pay, Google Pay, and other payment providers. Revenue growth also remains relatively modest, while the company needs to prove that its operational improvements can drive stronger top-line growth.

For now, the majority of analysts rate the stock a hold, with an average target price of $57.10, which implies only about 5% upside. It also trades at a forward P/E of just 9.7 times, as investors weigh the risks of its turnaround.

With SoFi and PayPal raising their outlooks, the question now is which stock offers the more compelling opportunity for investors.

Both SoFi and PayPal gave investors reasons to be optimistic after raising their 2026 forecasts. However, SoFi has a stronger growth case thanks to its expanding financial ecosystem, rising customer adoption, and ambitious earnings outlook for 2027. PayPal offers a potentially attractive turnaround opportunity, but it still needs to prove that its various initiatives can accelerate growth.

For growth-focused investors, SoFi is the higher-risk, higher-reward pick. PayPal is the safer option for value seekers, thanks to its low valuation. Both could appeal to buyers at current valuations, given the upward revisions to their outlooks.

#3148. Shooting Video With Honor’s New Magic 9 Pro Max Lets You Feel Like a Movie Director

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Phone-maker Honor partners with the iconic cinema camera maker ARRI to enhance the look and color of videos recorded on its Magic 9 Pro Max.

While standing on the roof of the Griffith Observatory in Los Angeles for the first time, I pulled out my phone to commemorate the moment by filming a video that pans toward the Hollywood sign. And then I did it again, using a special cinema mode created by the legendary movie camera company ARRI to give it some old Hollywood flair. The second video had a grainier look and could have been shot in the 1960s, with the sky appearing teal.

This might look like a filter, but it’s actually ARRI’s Nostalgia look — one of many color configurations available on the company’s cinema cameras, which start at $80,000. I’m using it on a smartphone from the Chinese company Honor.

This Honor Magic 9 Pro Max, announced Wednesday, looks a lot like an iPhone 18 Pro Max, with a similar unibody metal design and two-tone back glass. I used the phone in a comforting moss green, but it also comes in shadow black and glacier silver.

Honor’s focus on video production underscores the increasing trend of smartphone use in studio environments. And the company is banking on its partnership with ARRI to help its Magic 9 Pro Max stand out among a number of phones with their own Hollywood pedigree — including the iPhone.

Even if you aren’t familiar with ARRI, you’ll likely know movies filmed with the company’s cameras, such as 2022’s Everything Everywhere All at Once and 1947’s Dark Passage, starring Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall. ARRI’s cameras are designed for movie sets and priced accordingly, costing $65,000 to upward of $95,000 new. Instead of creating a cheaper camera, ARRI is bringing its color technology to the Magic 9 Pro Max’s camera app, which includes a dedicated ARRI Cinema mode.

This cinema mode uses the phone’s 200-megapixel wide and 200-megapixel telephoto cameras and lets you capture video with a wider 2.39:1 aspect ratio — similar to what’s used in theatrical releases. Cinema geeks may be particularly interested in the mode’s access to ARRI’s Look Library and its ability to install LUT files. Some are preloaded, while others can be downloaded from Honor’s and ARRI’s websites.

To put it as simply as I can, Looks and LUT files allow you to record video with a variety of cinema-like looks, including settings that can closely mimic an ARRI Alexa camera.

During a media demonstration at ARRI’s Los Angeles facility, two different film sets were recorded by both an Alexa camera and a Magic 9 Pro Max with similar looks and LUT settings. Both sets had ideal lighting, but the recorded footage showed similar color shading and detail. An ARRI rep pointed out that you have to look at the fine details, like the shadows of a bookshelf, to see the differences between the phone and cinema camera. Clearly, the Alexa camera was far better at capturing the scene, as it should.

Using the Magic 9 Pro Max, I filmed my own faux rainy-evening scene featuring dark green walls, a brown set and two actors speaking to each other. While I do like the set’s movie-like look, I was more impressed when I shuffled through the different ARRI Looks while watching the sunset at Griffith Observatory. Like the iPhone’s Photographic Styles for still images, ARRI Looks offer plenty of choices for video, including several black-and-white options. It’s fun to know that they’re the same options available to camera teams using ARRI’s full-fledged cinema cameras.

Honor hasn’t shared the Magic 9 Pro Max’s price or release date, but it won’t be coming to the US. However, it does have quite the spec list beyond its ARRI Cinema mode, including a 6.8-inch display, an 8,000-mAh battery with 100-watt wired charging and 80-watt wireless charging. The phone’s powered by the new Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor.

A 50-megapixel ultrawide camera joins the wide and telephoto cameras, but it doesn’t support the ARRI Cinema mode. The 55-megapixel front-facing camera uses a square sensor, like Center Stage on recent iPhones, allowing vertical selfies whether you’re holding the phone vertically or horizontally. Honor said this is a first for Android. I’m hopeful that more Android phone companies will bring this feature to their front-facing cameras in 2027.

The phone also ships with Android 17 and Honor’s MagicOS 11 overlay (it looks a lot like iOS 27), and joins other Android phones with support for Apple’s AirDrop via Quick Share.

As it stands, Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Max is being used in some baseball broadcasts, and the 2025 film 28 Years Later was shot primarily using the iPhone 15 Pro Max. Honor’s partnership with ARRI might lead to more cinema-quality features on smartphones, especially if more productions decide the pocket-sized camera is the right way to tell more big-screen stories.

Editors’ note: Mike Sorrentino’s travel costs for the Honor event were covered by Honor. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

Many of these games are free, and you can play them as many times as you want.

The popular word game Wordle is five years old, and it’s still popular. Josh Wardle launched the game in 2021 before The New York Times bought the game the following year. Since then, millions of people are estimated to play the game each day. If you want help with the daily game, CNET’s Gael Cooper has loads of tips and tricks to help you tackle each NYT Wordle puzzle, as well as solutions to each one.

Once you finish your Wordle, you’ll have to be patient and wait until the next day for the next puzzle. Thankfully, there are plenty of other word and puzzle games to choose from if you’re still craving a challenge. And some of these games let you play as many times as you want in a day.

Here are 10 other puzzle games you can play now for a fun challenge.

Another New York Times-owned puzzle, Connections is a tricky word game. “Players must select four groups of four words without making more than four mistakes,” the New York Times explained on X. There are also four color-coded difficulty levels for each game; yellow is the easiest, then green, then blue and finally purple. The game is also similar to the BBC quiz show Only Connect, and the show’s host took to X to point out the connection. See what I did there?

You can play Connections on any web browser, but you need a New York Times subscription (which starts at $1 a week) to play.

Strands is another New York Times-owned puzzle but this game resembles a word search more so than Wordle and Connections. This game presents a theme every day to help you find words in a grid. In Strands words can appear forward, backward, top-to-bottom or any number of ways in a traditional word search, and words can also form in the shape of an “L” or have a zigzag in them. When you find a word, tap the first letter and drag your finger to the other letters. Every letter in the puzzle is used, so if you still have letters that aren’t connected to words, you aren’t finished yet.

You can play Strands on any web browser but you need a New York Times subscription (again, $1 a week) to play.

You can play Quartiles on an iPhone or iPad but you need an Apple News subscription (which starts at $13 a month) to play.

Quordle has you solve four word puzzles at once, which sounds daunting.

Each of these word games resembles Wordle, but they add more rows, columns and words to solve. Each game requires you to simultaneously solve a different number of words at once: Dordle has you solving two words, Quordle four at once, Octordle eight at once and Sedecordle a whopping 16. Good luck.

You can play Dordle, Quordle, Octordle or Sedecordle on any web browser.

“Lewdle is a game about rude words,” this game’s content advisory reads. “If you’re likely to be offended by the use of profanity, vulgarity or obscenity, it likely isn’t for you.” Translation: It’s Wordle but with bad words. The words range from mild — like poopy — to words that would make a sailor blush. Thankfully, despite this game’s content warning, slurs are not included. Like Wordle, gray, yellow and green blocks are used in the same way and there’s only one puzzle per day. So go forth and let the bad words flow!

You can play Lewdle on any web browser. You can also download this game from Apple’s App Store or the Google Play store.

Not off to a great start with this Antiwordle puzzle.

Tired of seeing those gray, yellow and green blocks plastered all over your social media feed? Give Antiwordle a try. While Wordle wants you to guess a word in as few tries as possible, Antiwordle wants you to avoid the word by guessing as many times as possible. When you guess, letters will turn gray, yellow or red. Gray means the letter isn’t in the word and can’t be used again, yellow means the letter is in the word and must be included in each subsequent guess and red means the letter is in the exact position within the word and is locked in place. If you can use every letter on the keyboard without getting the word correct, you win. Honestly, I’ve found this version of Wordle to be much harder than the original.

You can play Antiwordle on any web browser.

Absurdle bills itself as the “adversarial version” of Wordle. While Wordle nudges you in the right direction with each guess, Absurdle is trying to avoid giving you the correct answer. According to the game’s website, “With each guess, Absurdle reveals as little information as possible, changing the secret word if need be.” Absurdle doesn’t pick a word at the beginning of the game for the player to guess. Instead, it uses the player’s guesses to narrow its list of words down in an effort to make the game go as long as possible. The final word might not even include a yellow letter from one of your earlier guesses either. You can guess as many times as you want, which is helpful, and the best score you can get is four. Have fun!

You can play Absurdle on any web browser.

For more word game fun, check out CNET’s Wordle tips and everything you need to know about the word game. You can also check out what to know about the other New York Times-owned games, Connections and Strands.

#3143. UnitedHealth shares are doing something unusual ahead of earnings

The only thing more expensive than health insurance is perhaps the costs of insuring shares of health insurers. Case in point: UnitedHealth Group, which reports earnings Tuesday.

Implied volatility is running at twice realized volatility ahead of the October 13 quarterly earnings release. In other words, options prices - the cost of insuring the underlying stock - are expensive, which sets up well for short premium strategies.

In the case of UnitedHealth shares, traders can sell November premium to cut the cost of a longer-dated January call by more than half. UnitedHealth heads into Tuesday's report with much of the damage from its prior missteps already priced in. While rising healthcare costs always remain a headwind, management's 13% to 16% EPS growth target looks achievable. The stock has basically been flat over the last five years.

By the way, according to the company, 90% of United's 52 million customers worldwide are in the U.S. By its own statistics, the company covers about 12% to 13.5% of the U.S. population.

Growing enrollment is critical to EPS growth, but so too is underwriting margin. In the managed care and health insurance business, underwriting margin represents the core operational profitability generated directly from managing healthcare risk. It measures the financial return an insurer achieves strictly from collecting premiums and managing medical care. On the enrollment side, ACA marketplace-driven enrollment appears poised to decline, a headwind for revenue in a segment that had been a growth driver. Fortunately, it's a smaller piece of the enterprise than Medicare and Commercial. Commercial fee-based enrollment grew ~2.9% YoY between 2024 and 2025, while total Medicare enrollment grew 4.5%. The commercial segment growth may not look impressive as a headline number, but given the U.S. workforce grew ~1.4% over the same period, United appears to be gaining market share.

At 17 times forward earnings, and with free cash flow at 5.7% of enterprise value and 6.5% of market cap, the stock isn't priced for any recovery. On the options side, the market is implying 40% volatility for a stock that's been realizing 20%. Granted. The 40% number captures this week's earnings, and it's likely elevated because the stock has had a couple of eye-watering earnings moves in the past 8 reported quarters. In January, the stock fell almost 20% following earnings, and April 2025 saw a similar sharp decline.

As it stands, UNH is about 12-13% below the midpoint of the two-year high and low. The stock has traded lower in five of the last 8 earnings. Current options prices imply a 6.5% earnings move, according to Cboe LiveVol data. That's the second highest implied move in almost two years.

Sell the November 340/420 strangle to help finance the purchase of the January 2027 400 call. Buying the Jan 400 call costs $18.20. If UNH finishes November between 340 and 420, both short legs expire worthless and the January call is held for $7.60, with a breakeven of $407.60 at January expiration. A rally through 420 is covered by the long 400 call. The real risk is below: a close under 340 means buying shares there, for an effective basis near $347.60 including the debit.

#3141. The Switch 2 Zelda: Ocarina of Time Is a Brilliant Remake

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

It’s back, completely refreshed, and an absolute joy to experience again.

It was way back in 1998 when I finished Ocarina of Time. I remember how incredible it all was, not only to play but also to look at. N64 games back then felt stunning — so impressive that I rushed out to make the N64 the first Nintendo home console I ever owned.

Those days are gone, and N64 games now look pretty rough to my eyes. But with the $60 Ocarina of Time remake, exclusive to the Switch 2, Nintendo brings some of that magic back again; I’ve never had more fun replaying a game in my life.

When I first tried the new version of Ocarina for about an hour a few weeks ago, it felt like it was replacing my old memories of playing the original game. More than a week into playing at home, I can confirm that the remake has completely replaced my memories of the original. I’ve revisited the N64 version a few times through the Switch Online N64 app, but it feels so minimal and awkward compared to the remake that I can’t go back now.

But it’s also brought me right back to the feeling I had in 1998. Like in the game itself, I’ve been whisked back in time to reexperience the past — and it’s better than it’s ever been. I’ve been down the Ocarina rerelease road before, when the 3DS version arrived in 2011, but the Switch 2 version is far more impressive. It’s not a new game, but at times it almost feels like one.

Everything in Ocarina of Time has been created fresh again. Like some sort of set builder making all the pieces of an old show from memory, it’s astonishing how Ocarina is an old game made with completely redone graphics. It outdoes Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom in visual splendor, with similarly gorgeous open vistas at every turn.

Just as Ocarina of Time inspired Breath of the Wild, it’s Breath of the Wild that’s now reshaped Ocarina — at least visually. The scope, story and challenges in Ocarina remain just about the same, creating a more intimate experience despite its sense of epic scale. If you’ve never played it before, think of it as a theme park version of the supersized Hyrule in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

But I appreciate its more contained scale even more now. I got lost in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, and not always in a good way. To be honest, at times, parts of those games began to feel repetitive. Ocarina of Time’s story is told more directly, with clearly laid-out goals and a faster pace. It feels like a true fusion of the sandbox-like open worlds of recent Zelda games and the intricate, puzzle-driven storylines of older ones.

I’d love this new Ocarina even if it only brought updated graphics, reworked sound and new voice acting, which grew on me. But its control scheme makes the game far more intuitive to play. The old Ocarina didn’t have a jump button: Link just auto-jumped! Here, you can jump anywhere. The old game never had a second analog stick to control your viewing angle; it relied on “Z-targeting” to look ahead or recenter your focus on objects and enemies. Now, you can look around and Z-target with a trigger button — something that modern Zelda players probably just take for granted.

Some areas are different now: Early on in Kokiri Forest, the way you find the first sword is different. The dialogue has also changed. That’s just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the many little shifts here, which become hard to notice. At some point, my experience of the new 2026 version simply took over and overwrote all my old, fuzzy memories of the 1998 version. It’s now, once again, the game as it felt to me back then.

Maybe it’s that I’m getting older, or I don’t replay games such as Ocarina of Time year after year as some do, but I realize I forgot a lot of what happens in this game. But I look forward to every night I get a chance to play it again. It’s that good.

I didn’t think that would happen, not with RPGs and Zelda games advancing so much over the years. It’s a testament to Ocarina of Time that its structure and mystery still feel perfectly paced. There are tons of side missions, but the main story arc is strong and continuous. I felt a sense of awe more than once, even when it came to things I knew would happen. The time travel — which I hope doesn’t spoil too much for anyone who’s never played before, though, hey, it is called Ocarina of Time — still feels wondrous.

I was skeptical about Nintendo spending all its resources updating classic games over the last year or so — a trend that started with Star Fox, continued with Switch Sports Resort and has returned here. I wanted new games for the Switch 2 — not retreads. But I have to admit that Nintendo has done these remakes with expert care. And in the case of Ocarina of Time, the effort truly feels like it transcends the original. As much as I ended up loving Star Fox again, it never felt as much like a new game as this Ocarina remake does.

Is it a truly new game? No. But it feels like the most singular Zelda game again, taking precedence even over Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom. And with its graphic overhaul, it now feels like a cousin to those games in a new way, a sort of trilogy (but not exactly). I find myself, once again, appreciating how absurd and adorable all the characters are. Zelda games have such a goofy sense of humor, and I feel like Ocarina does more than Breath and Tears do. I’ve gotten a kick out of finding every side character in Hyrule just to see their new faces.

And the dungeons in Ocarina of Time are so good. I want Zelda games to return to the kind of intricate, puzzle-filled dungeons found here.

I’m so stunned by how much I love the new Ocarina that I’m wondering what magic Nintendo could work on other throwbacks. Do this for Mario 64, or Pilotwings.

The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask is the “other” Zelda game for N64, and it’s even more brilliantly conceived. Remaking it for the Switch 2 now seems like a when — not an if — considering Ocarina’s Hyrule has been completely rebuilt with new graphics. Nintendo brought Ocarina and Majora to 3DS, and the cycle could repeat again here. I’d be all for it.

Could this all be a massive test run for a future Zelda that doesn’t exist yet? It certainly feels like it — but when? The remastered version of Metroid Prime paved the way for Metroid Prime 4‘s release. Beyond the battle-focused Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment, this is the first Zelda game made exclusively with the Switch 2’s hardware in mind — and its lush visuals show it. It’s the best-looking game on the Switch 2 yet, and naturally, it makes me wonder what a new Zelda game could feel like. Or heck, a new Mario.

This reconstruction of Ocarina of Time feels like it’s strutting, dripping with luxury, full of glorious style, a symphony played with a full orchestra. And somehow, unleashing it all in service of a fantastic remake doesn’t feel excessive. I’m having a blast playing it, but I also want to see what this opens up for the next generation of Nintendo Switch 2 games.

But if you’ve never played a Zelda game before and have a Switch 2, I envy you: The new Ocarina of Time is an incredible place to start.

#3140. Is Claude Code truly faster with message threads? I did the math on my logs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Claude Code’s update could save you time during demanding, hours-long coding sessions at no extra cost. But by how much? Here's my real-world result.

Anthropic yesterday introduced message threads as part of Claude’s Messages API. Don’t confuse message threads with traditional human-to-human discussion threads. With message threads, entire conversations no longer have to be resent with each API call, saving roughly 35% of time-to-first-token when Claude requests contain 500,000 to 1 million tokens.

This feature is on by default for most Claude Code users. API users can turn it on using the “thread” parameter for API requests.

Token consumption remains unchanged, so this capability doesn’t provide a cost savings. The 35% savings is Anthropic’s measurement.

Also: Claude Code’s revised projects adds AI orchestration, but local developers must wait

Timing data from roughly 980 turns in my own Claude Code logs before this feature became available shows that Claude usually began a response about 3 seconds after each mid-task request when running contexts of 500,000 tokens and up. During five busy evenings last month, my conversations made roughly 100 to 225 model calls in a four hour stretch.

Using Anthropic’s reported 35% median time-to-first token reduction in a quick projection, Claude estimated a 2- to 4-minute savings per four hour work session.

Agents often send a bunch of requests to the model during each conversation. Before message threads, each message sent the entire conversation with each request.

Imagine if you’re in a very long texting chat with a friend. Now imagine if every time you sent a text to that friend, you also had to send every other text and every other reply along with that original text. That’s how model messaging has always worked. Except now, with message threads, there’s a better way.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code – here’s why they choose it over Codex

With message threads turned on, agents only have to send what’s changed since the last turn. This reduces the amount of data transmission and increases responsiveness, what Anthropic calls time-to-first-token.

The benefit is seen most strongly in sessions that have a context of 500,000 to a 1 million tokens. About half of my sessions hit that context ceiling multiple times a night.

Anthropic reports that Claude’s message threads reduce median time-to-first-token by 35% for large requests. While my estimated savings of several minutes per session isn’t huge, the benefit increases with very long-running coding agents, and agents that transmit documents and image-heavy workloads.

For computer-using agents, all those screenshots “stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn,” according to the Anthropic blog post on the feature.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code

While the time savings may not seem huge, in larger enterprise deployments or deployments where you want the AI to respond faster, any reduction in latency is a big deal and will be seen in any application of Claude technology that has a lot of back-and-forth turns with large data payloads.

Even though the addition of threads to the Messages API can reduce latency, token usage and therefore cost won’t go down. That’s because the model itself will still process the full conversation during every turn. Rate limits also don’t change.

Message threads and prompt caching can work together to reduce workload. Prompt caching has been around for about two years now, and it does save money. That’s because prompt caching allows the model to avoid re-processing prompts over and over (for example, in looping analysis calls).

On the other hand, the message threads capability does offer an extra smidge of performance, at no extra cost. So, there’s that.

Context is the size of the full session that Claude is currently working with. The rough human equivalent is current working or short-term memory. Most Claude Code sessions max out at a million token context, where a locally-hosted AI on my 128GB Mac Studio handles a context no bigger than 64K, or about 6% of the Claude Code context size.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

Compaction is a process where the AI attempts to reduce and eliminate extra information to fit the current session’s turns into the available context. An oversimplified analog is when you save a JPEG with quality turned way down in order to save space. You lose a lot of the visual fidelity, but you still get the main idea.

The larger the context you have, the longer you can go before the session has to initiate compaction. But there’s a gotcha. The larger the context you have, the more chance there is the model will lose track of what it’s working on or make reasoning errors.

Individual one-off requests also won’t see an improvement from message threads. Also, any conversation that delays longer than 5 minutes between turns will send the full message contents and not just the new stuff.

This feature doesn’t eliminate context management or compaction. But if your context is quite large, it will make responses a bit snappier.

Overall, message threads are a good thing, a solid if small innovation that increases responsiveness. While the feature doesn’t reduce costs, there’s also no additional cost for the additional performance, which is itself a win.

#3139. So You Bought an iPhone 18 Pro. Do You Still Need a Real Camera?

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Apple's phone takes beautiful photos, but is it as good as using a Fujifilm X-M5?

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe

The iPhone 18 Pro is among the most accomplished phone cameras around, packing an array of sensors and lenses that are all capable of taking stunning images in a variety of conditions. Throw in the new creative tweaks to Apple’s Photographic Styles and the iPhone 18 Pro becomes a formidable partner to serious photographers.

But how does it compare to an actual camera? To see why you’d pick one over the other, I took the iPhone 18 Pro on some photo walks alongside Fujifilm’s X-M5, a compact-sized mirrorless camera with interchangeable lenses and a host of filmic profiles to choose from.

This isn’t designed to be a direct comparison between each specific model — after all, a phone has other advantages beyond a camera, some of which I’ll come to later. I’m not going to pixel peep at ultrafine details nor estimate which has the technically best dynamic range. This is more about which allows you to be more creative and more engaged in your image-taking and what each one offers.

With the iPhone 16 Pro Apple brought its Photographic Styles with the grid-like tool for adjusting the color tones and shadow depth for each of the looks. It was a huge boon to iPhone photographers who want to shoot with a specific look without having to manually edit each image after the fact. Apple took that further on the 18 Pro by bringing in more advanced tools, including the ability to add image grain and bloom to your images and giving manual control over white balance. Finally.

Fujifilm, meanwhile, has won the hearts of millions of photographers the world over with the ability to create filmic styles that can be shared and installed as “recipes” on its cameras. Like Photographic Styles, these looks change everything from color tones to film grain and allow you to shoot with an almost infinite array of filmic styles with no editing required.

In practice, both operate in much the same way. On the iPhone, I erred toward warmer styles such as Amber and Gold, bringing the shadows down and adding some film grain. My Kodak Gold-inspired Fujifilm recipes aimed to achieve a similar effect and while they’re not identical, I can’t say I like either one of them over the other.

I don’t like all of the iPhone’s styles, but there are a lot of Fujifilm recipes I don’t like either, and arguably this just comes down to personal taste anyway. But I have noticed that there’s a lot that Apple can do to improve Styles for photographers.

For one, you can’t save a specific style as a preset to recall later. While you can tell the phone to remember your last-used settings each time you open it, if you change those settings, you’ll need to remember what they originally were if you want to go back. It also means it’s difficult to share those presets with others, whereas Fujifilm camera owners have created a vast community sharing recipes far and wide.

Overall, Fujifilm’s recipes give much finer control over the look of your image and make it easier to recall a certain preset when you want to start shooting away. Both the iPhone and X-M5 (and indeed almost all regular cameras) also allow you to shoot images in raw format too, allowing you to apply your own edits later on in apps like Adobe Lightroom, Snapseed or VSCO.

The iPhone’s size makes it the dream camera for street or travel photography where you may be walking for miles every day and don’t want to be weighed down by equipment. It just slips into your pocket and can be whipped out just as easily when inspiration strikes. While Fujifilm’s X-M5 is small for a camera, with a lens on you’ll struggle to get it into a pocket, meaning you’ll need a dedicated camera bag to carry it around — or have it around your neck on a strap, which could become uncomfortable after a full day out.

That’s doubly the case if you have extra lenses you’d want to take with you, which the iPhone has built in. Even Fujifilm’s endlessly popular fixed-lens X100VI is still big enough that you’ll only manage to get it into a large coat pocket at best.

On the other hand, cameras are built to be ergonomic when taking images. Their larger sizes give you something to grip onto and hold steady. By comparison, holding a skinny iPhone when taking a photo can often feel delicate, especially when you’re trying not to accidentally press on the screen. Personally, I don’t enjoy the feel of taking photos with a phone, and it’s one of the reasons why I’d always reach for a real camera over a phone for a day’s photography.

That’s especially true when it comes to adjusting shooting settings. Changing exposure compensation means multiple taps on the phone’s screen. Ditto if you want to change white balance or shutter speed. Most cameras like the X-M5 or X100VI offer physical controls to instantly change settings when out shooting in the field, often without even needing to look, saving you crucial seconds when capturing the decisive moment.

While Fujifilm’s popular X100VI has a fixed lens offering a constant 35mm focal length, the X-M5 — along with many others in the range — has interchangeable lenses, allowing it to swap between a plethora of lenses from both Fujifilm and a wealth of third parties. Whether you want an ultrawide fisheye lens, a super-long telephoto for wildlife shots or creative lenses like PolarPro’s LightLeaks lenses, there’s an option out there.

But that means spending more money on more gear and then having to carry an increasingly heavy kit bag out on location to use all that fancy new glass. The iPhone has its multiple lenses built right in. Its focal lengths include 13mm, 24mm, 28mm, 35mm, 48mm, 100mm and 200mm, all from one pocket-sized device.

Sure, most of those include some kind of digital cropping or upscaling and the quality isn’t what you’d find from a pro-standard telephoto zoom lens, but for most people who want to take snaps out and about in the street, the iPhone’s lens options essentially put a full kit-bag of gear into your pocket.

If you do want more lens options for your iPhone, there are a range of add-ons you can pick up. I love shooting with Moment’s clip-on lenses, especially the anamorphic lens for video and the macro lens for close-up work. Then there’s PolarPro’s various filters, like the Everyday filter, which is the same one I slapped onto the front of the X-M5.

As Apple’s phones are so popular, accessories for them are the easiest to come by compared to almost any other Android phone. But the same can be said for Fujifilm’s camera — and most other compact cameras around. Alongside the aforementioned armada of lens choices, you can also pick up thumb grips and half cases to customize the camera and things like flashes and tripods for taking your photography further.

The iPhone, of course, has the benefit of also being a smartphone. It’s not just a camera, meaning that when you’re done taking your photos you’ve got the option to instantly edit them in whatever apps you like and share them to Instagram or over WhatsApp without first having to transfer them to your computer.

But for me that’s also one of the biggest downsides of using a phone as a camera. I’ve written about this before, but the problem essentially boils down to wanting to focus on one task at a time. A camera has just one function: taking pictures. I pick it up to do one thing and that’s all I have to pay attention to.

When I’m shooting with my phone, I can be bombarded with incoming notifications, phone calls and other pop-ups, all of which are desperate to take my attention away from the act and craft of shooting photos. I love having a great phone camera with me for those occasions when I want a photo and I’m not carrying a camera, but when I want to be purposeful in my photography and plan to head out to shoot work I’m proud of, it will always be a dedicated camera that I’ll reach for.

Which is best for you depends on two factors: Your budget and how serious you are about your photography. The iPhone is a superb camera phone for out-and-about snaps and while it’s certainly possible to take pro-level photos with it, it’s not always as easy to use — or as inspirational — as using a proper smaller camera like a Fujifilm X-M5, X100VI or other models like a Ricoh GRIV, Leica Q3 43 or even a small mirrorless camera.

Plus, if you’re keen for a great all-round imaging experience and you don’t have the cash for two tech purchases right now, going all in on just an iPhone 18 Pro is a smart move. But if you want to take a more authentic and intentional approach to your photography and feel creatively inspired by holding a physical camera and twiddling real, analog dials will absolutely benefit from looking toward adding a camera like the Fujifilm X-M5 or X100VI to your photography arsenal.

CNET Editor at Large Katie Collins found that when she used a proper camera on a big trip to China instead of just her phone, it rekindled her passion for photography that had long sat dormant.

While smartphone photography has come on in leaps and bounds in the past few years, there’s still nothing that beats that feeling of lifting a real camera to your eye and firing that shutter button.

#3138. This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

You won't see the 'suspended' sign because it's not meant for you.

KELA researchers have exposed an active financial-scam infrastructure that hosts hundreds of fraudulent websites capable of faking their own suspensions to stay online. As of Oct. 25, 2026, 248 financial scam and phishing domains tied to 189 major US banks and financial services have been linked to the same infrastructure.

According to the cybersecurity firm’s report, published on Tuesday, the “Suspended” infrastructure operation runs websites that have cloned the official domains of victim organizations, with a particular focus on business banking. Many domains use the [keyword]-[bank].com format, slotting in keywords such as “secure,” “disable,” “protect,” and “cancel.”

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

A handful of servers spread across two shared hosting providers run the backend of Suspended infrastructure, which has also been tied to phishing campaigns targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and government services in the UK, the Netherlands, Australia, and New Zealand. As a result, the researchers believe that either a single operator is behind the setup or that the server infrastructure is part of a wider phishing-as-a-service platform.

This phishing campaign stands out because of how the cybercriminals behind the scam are protecting it: by issuing takedown notices.

When you visit a website and see a message that it has been taken down or suspended, it’s usually because the domain has been associated with malicious or illegal activity, including phishing and scams. Law enforcement agencies, often with help from technology firms, find these websites, obtain the necessary court orders, and seize the infrastructure or accounts behind them to force a suspension through a registrar or hosting provider.

You see the notice, you move on — and this also goes for scanners and security teams.

However, in this case, the scam artists created a mechanism to show it themselves, to avoid being flagged and taken down. But it’s when they show it that matters.

The false suspension notice appears deceptively simple at first glance. A phishing kit embedded in the domain registers the IP address of each visitor, and on their second visit, they are shown a fake “account suspended” page. The kit is disguised as a challenge page similar to those legitimately used by Cloudflare.

Researchers also detected other decoys, including “Sorry, you’ve been blocked” notices, blank pages, and redirections to Google. Some pages also have reCAPTCHAs, and the researchers detected scripts that block browser developer tools, likely to slow analysis.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages – here’s how

But why show fake suspension notices in the first place? To scanners and cybersecurity teams, it looks like someone else has already dealt with the malicious domain, and they can move on to the next suspicious website.

“That design targets exactly the people who could shut a site down,” KELA says. “A victim typically follows a link once. A scanner, a security team or a takedown provider checks a reported site and then checks it again to confirm, and the second check shows what looks like a completed takedown.”

As shown in the image below, while scanners would detect a suspension notice, victims would still see the cloned website, complete with lures to entice them into entering their information, leading to financial fraud and potentially identity theft. After all, one visit is enough.

As of this writing, there are 248 live domains, plus those taken offline after the researchers disclosed their findings to law enforcement; over 300 scam domains have been hosted on the same infrastructure since May this year. Unfortunately, this phishing campaign remains active, with new domains appearing every day.

One lead could reveal the operator: a remote desktop connection to the malicious infrastructure through a standard UK home broadband connection, but it has not been verified.

Use a phishing link checker to verify whether a URL is trustworthy, and remember that any email or message claiming to be from your bank may be fraudulent.

Typical signs of a bank phishing email include:

When it comes to organizations, KELA has released a free Bank Phishing Check tool that compares official domains and organizations against the websites uncovered during the firm’s research.

#3137. Gilead Sciences Has Raised Its Dividend for 11 Straight Years. Here's Why the Streak Looks Safe.

Gilead Sciences increased its quarterly dividend by 3.8% this year.

Gilead Sciences (GILD +4.19%) is the leading pharmaceutical company that produces HIV treatments. Its chronic HIV management therapies are largely insulated from macroeconomic downturns because of how crucial they are to those with the disease.

Gilead raised its quarterly dividend by 3.8% this year to $0.82, the 11th consecutive year it has increased its dividend. The dividend yield, at Gilead's current share price, is around 1.9%, nearly double the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.58%) average. The company has increased its dividend by just under 75% over the past decade.

Gilead is in a great position to continue raising its dividend. Let's see why.

Gilead's cash dividend payout ratio is only 29.8%, indicating it has ample room to maintain its dividend and fund other operations.

The driver of that cash is the company's HIV franchise. In the third quarter, the company reported $8.3 billion in revenue, up 13% year over year, led by 18% higher HIV sales compared to the same period a year ago and HIV prevention therapies, whose sales nearly doubled year over year.

Over nine months, the company reported $10.6 billion in free cash flow, up 68% year over year.

In recent years, Gilead has expanded into oncology and anti-inflammatory treatments. It just opened a new research center to grow its oncology, inflammation, and research data science, and it has said it plans to spend $32 billion in projects through 2030 to support research.

Trodelvy, used to treat bladder cancer and breast cancer, brought in $506 million in the third quarter, up 42% year over year. The drug was also recently approved as a combination therapy with Keytruda, made by Merck, as a first-line treatment for a very aggressive form of breast cancer.

The company also has more than a dozen inflammation and immunology drugs in clinical testing, most notably emvistegrast, which recently showed a 66% response rate in patients with ulcerative colitis.

James Halley has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Gilead Sciences and Merck. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.
